title: Empirical Evaluation of a Generate–Validate–Repair Loop for Intent→Network Configuration Using a Deterministic Reachability Validator
abstract: We measure the marginal effect of wrapping a single LLM generator (declared gpt-5-mini) with a deterministic reachability validator plus at most one automated repair (a GVR loop) on intent→device‑configuration tasks. Using a preregistered paired shared‑initial design (cns‑m2026‑01) with N=300 intents (600 episodes), the baseline generator produced execution‑validated correct configurations in 299/300 tasks (99.667%); the guarded pipeline (validator ± one repair) produced 300/300 (100.0%). Paired difference = 0.003333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap‑percentile CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). Provider‑call accounting: 301 model calls (300 generator calls + 1 repair call). All model calls, validator traces, scoring JSON, manifests, and analysis artifacts are archived with SHA‑256 hashes; representative artifact paths and SHA values are cited in the Disclosure Statement and in‑text. We interpret the result in light of a near‑ceiling baseline, describe operational implications, and document threats to validity and complete reproducibility instructions based on the archived artifacts.

sections.introduction:
Generative LLMs are being integrated into NetOps pipelines to translate operator intent into low‑level device configuration. Typical production architectures add a deterministic validator (reachability/policy checker) that prevents unsafe proposals from being applied and optionally triggers automated repair. Engineering reports document many such prototypes, but rigorous, preregistered paired measurements of the marginal effect of a validator+repair wrapper are scarce, and reproducible archival of every model call and validator trace is uncommon.

We address this by executing a fully preregistered paired experiment (cns‑m2026‑01) that measures whether a deterministic reachability validator plus at most one automated repair increases the paired rate of correct, safely executable configurations compared with the same LLM generator alone. The design uses shared‑initial semantics (one generator proposal per intent reused for both conditions) to isolate the gate’s marginal effect. Our deliverables include the complete preregistration, the full execution manifest, per‑episode scoring JSON, provider‑call traces, call cache, validator traces, and the full analysis log; representative SHA‑256 values and artifact paths are given in the Disclosure Statement. The principal empirical result and all descriptive statistics reported below are deterministically reproducible from those archived artifacts.
sections.related_work: Recent NetOps and AIOps literature explores intent→configuration synthesis, verifier‑assisted pipelines, and generate–validate–repair (GVR) architectures. Representative engineering and research leads motivated our protocol and are cited for positioning. Prior work typically demonstrates prototypes and success rates but often lacks (i) preregistered paired designs that isolate marginal gate effects, (ii) per‑call provider and validator trace archival, and (iii) deterministic reproducibility metadata. We follow best‑practice recommendations from contemporary LLM evaluation surveys: preregistration of estimands, automated contamination checks for public data, fixed RNG seeds for selection and bootstrap, and archival of all intermediate artifacts and hashes.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands. The study was preregistered as cns‑m2026‑01. The preregistration froze the research question, primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), paired shared‑initial design, task selection and contamination rules, maximum repair budget (≤1 automated repair call per intent), retry policy, confirmatory test (exact McNemar two‑sided), and bootstrap CI plan (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). Preregistration SHA‑256: 0726a6c02c1ed6fc379927f4bb0696330f0b00484f15caee5cf4ebc072316bf7.

Task bank, selection, and contamination controls. We constructed a 300‑intent corpus via an automated pipeline that combined filtered public intent→configuration candidates and deterministic synthetic templates to satisfy preregistered strata. The pipeline applied deterministic contamination heuristics (exact‑string and k‑token shingle overlap) and excluded items above thresholds; the final task manifest is archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl — SHA‑256: 91564bb6...). Inclusion/exclusion decisions and counts are logged in the execution manifest.

Generator, validator, and guarded pipeline. Declared generator: gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json — SHA‑256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). The guarded pipeline invokes deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator v5.0). The validator parses candidate configurations into typed commands, simulates device‑state transitions on a closed emulator snapshot, enforces task constraints (allowed_touched_fields, preserve_unspecified_state, required_group constraints), and emits a pass/fail plus a structured trace. If the validator fails, the pipeline allows one automated repair call; repair attempts and the repair prompt/response are archived when used. All validator traces and scoring JSON are archived per episode (execution/scoring/*.json).

Execution contract and provider accounting. The preregistered contract stipulated: task_count = 300, planned_episode_count = 600 (shared initial reused across conditions), maximum_model_calls = 600, and a retry policy permitting up to two automated retries for transient infra failures. Missingness rules excluded pairs where both conditions could not be executed. The actual run completed 600 episodes with zero failures. Provider‑call accounting indicates 301 model calls used (300 generator calls + 1 repair call). Full provider traces and call cache entries are archived (execution/provider_calls/, execution/call_cache/).

Scoring and confirmatory analysis. Episode outcome is binary: 1 = execution‑validated configuration that satisfies the intent and produces no unintended reachability or policy changes; 0 otherwise. The primary inferential test is the exact McNemar two‑sided test on discordant pairs (n10, n01). Complementary uncertainty quantification uses a bootstrap‑percentile 95% CI for the paired difference (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). The pre‑registered analysis executor 'paired_binary_analysis_v1' produced the confirmatory numbers and logs archived in analysis/ (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl — SHA‑256: 7db06f53...).
sections.results:
Execution accounting. Planned episodes = 600 (300 intents × 2 conditions). Completed episodes = 600; failed episodes = 0. Provider calls used = 301 (300 generator calls + 1 repair call). All per‑episode artifacts and provider traces are archived and referenced below.

Aggregated outcomes. Condition aggregates (analysis/condition_summary.csv — SHA‑256: 55eacb88...): baseline successes = 299/300 (0.996667); guarded successes = 300/300 (1.0).

Paired contingency and inference (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv — SHA‑256: 3421adb5...). The observed contingency: n11=299, n10=1 (baseline=0, guarded=1), n01=0 (baseline=1, guarded=0), n00=0. Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333333333332993. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap‑percentile 95% CI for the paired difference = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). These exact values and the analysis run parameters are archived (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl — SHA‑256: 7db06f53...). The exact McNemar p equals 1.0 here because discordant counts are extreme and the exact two‑sided enumeration yields a two‑sided probability of observing as or more extreme discrepancies given the null; the implementation and counts are available in the archived contingency CSV and analysis log for audit.

Repair and failure diagnostics. Repair‑iterations histogram: 299 tasks required zero repairs; 1 task required a single automated repair (guarded repair trace archived at execution/provider_calls/task-000117-guarded-repair.json — SHA‑256: 4deb410d5736ab332cd5caaf00b16051e5b0aef2276255c0770098f63cb523ba). No residual guarded failures remained. The failure‑mode taxonomy annotated by the scorer (validator violation, parse/syntax, emulator mismatch, specification ambiguity) is stored in per‑episode scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/). The single corrected discordant episode is traceable from the paired contingency to its scoring JSON and repair trace.

Representative episodes and forensic artifacts. Three representative episodes (pair‑000001, pair‑000002, pair‑000003) are provided as examples of validator traces and normalization; their shared initial proposals and scoring JSONs are archived (execution/responses/task‑00000X‑shared‑initial.txt and execution/scoring/task‑00000X‑baseline.json / guarded.json). For example, execution/responses/task‑000001‑shared‑initial.txt (SHA‑256 = 8f38c8be...) is identical under baseline and guarded for that intent; the corresponding scoring JSON documents the validator parse, simulated final states, and the valid normalization accepted by the validator.

Reproducibility checksum summary. Key artifact SHAs (representative): execution/raw_results.jsonl = 176776d1..., execution/task_manifest.jsonl = 91564bb6..., analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv = 3421adb5..., analysis/analysis_log.jsonl = 7db06f53..., execution/model_configuration.json = a40e96e2..., repair trace = 4deb410d.... The full execution manifest contains exhaustive per‑file SHA‑256 indices and is archived at execution/execution_manifest.json (path cited in the Disclosure Statement).
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and operational implications. The guarded GVR pipeline corrected the only isolated baseline failure at the cost of a single repair call. This demonstrates that a deterministic validator coupled with a limited repair budget can fix some generator mistakes while incurring minimal extra model‑call cost; provider accounting shows model_calls_used = 301 for 300 intents. However, the observed absolute paired improvement is small because the baseline generator already performed near ceiling on this controlled emulator corpus. In production, where base errors are more frequent or task difficulty is higher, the marginal benefit of a validator and repair loop can be larger. Operations teams should weigh expected baseline error rates, validator coverage (which properties are checked), repair budget, and cost/latency implications when designing an enforcement gate.

Why the exact McNemar p = 1.0. The exact two‑sided McNemar test depends on the distribution of discordant pairs (n10, n01). With n10=1 and n01=0, the small sample exact enumeration yields a two‑sided p of 1.0 for the chosen implementation. The raw counts, contingency CSV, and the analysis log that produced this p are archived (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256: 3421adb5...; analysis/analysis_log.jsonl SHA‑256: 7db06f53...). Readers can re‑compute alternative tests from the same archived contingency if they prefer different exact implementations or one‑sided tests.

Threats to validity (expanded). Internal validity: the shared‑initial design was preregistered and isolates the gate's marginal effect but is not identical to a pipeline that regenerates independent proposals per condition; this design choice should be considered when extrapolating to end‑to‑end systems that requery the LLM under different prompts or context. Construct validity: safety is operationalized as absence of emulator‑observed unintended reachability or policy changes in a closed snapshot; this is a useful proxy but does not capture every production risk (timing, vendor quirks, or unmodelled device behavior). External validity: single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) and a deterministic emulator limit generalizability; results do not imply equivalent outcomes for other LLMs, heterogeneous hardware, or live networks. Conclusion validity: the ceiling baseline reduces power to detect larger absolute improvements; we report exact counts, the contingency table, and bootstrap CI so readers can assess practical significance.

Reproducibility and future reanalysis. All raw model responses, provider‑call traces, validator traces, per‑episode scoring JSONs, call cache entries, task manifest, transformation manifest, and analysis logs are archived with SHA‑256; representative SHA values appear in the Disclosure Statement and the execution manifest. Using the archived per‑episode scoring JSONs, researchers can re‑compute any alternative paired statistic, recode outcome definitions, or simulate larger repair budgets without issuing new generator calls (note: hypothetical new repair calls were not executed and would require additional model calls). The archived repair trace for the single observed repair enables forensic inspection of the exact repair prompt and response. The registered analysis code and seeds used for bootstrap and the exact test are available in analysis/ (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl — SHA‑256 cited).
sections.conclusion: We ran a preregistered paired shared‑initial experiment (cns‑m2026‑01) to evaluate the marginal effect of a deterministic reachability validator and ≤1 automated repair on LLM‑generated intent→config proposals (N=300). Results: baseline success = 299/300 (0.996667), guarded success = 300/300 (1.0); paired difference = 0.003333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). Provider calls used = 301 (300 generator + 1 repair). The guarded pipeline corrected one isolated baseline error at small extra cost and produced full validator traces and archival evidence. The practical implication is that verifier‑assisted repair can materially reduce certain failure modes with limited overhead, but aggregate benefit depends on baseline error rates and validator coverage. All empirical claims are traceable to archived artifacts (paths and SHA‑256 values in the Disclosure Statement). Future work should test broader model families, richer validator models, and iterative repair budgets in higher‑error distributions to observe larger marginal effects.

disclosure_statement:
Disclosure Statement — archived provenance and runtime facts

Initial master prompt immutable reference (archived): provenance/master_prompt.txt — SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba.
Preregistration: cns‑m2026‑01 (preregistration SHA‑256 = 0726a6c02c1ed6fc379927f4bb0696330f0b00484f15caee5cf4ebc072316bf7). The preregistration froze the paired shared‑initial design, contamination/exclusion rules, retry policy, repair budget (≤1), confirmatory exact McNemar two‑sided test, and bootstrap CI plan (10,000 resamples, seed=1729).
Declared LLM(s) and model identifier: gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json — SHA‑256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). Provider traces and per‑call cache are archived under execution/provider_calls/ and execution/call_cache/ (full manifest indexed in execution/execution_manifest.json; representative provider‑call repair trace: execution/provider_calls/task-000117-guarded-repair.json — SHA‑256: 4deb410d5736ab332cd5caaf00b16051e5b0aef2276255c0770098f63cb523ba).
Orchestration and tools: adapter_family 'hosted_netops_gvr_v1' orchestrated generator→validator→(optional repair). Validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0); transformation and emulator‑snapshot identifiers are listed in execution/transformation_manifest.json (SHA‑256 archived). Execution used shared‑initial semantics (single generator proposal per intent reused in both conditions) as preregistered.
Artifact archival and reproducibility: every model response, provider‑call trace, scorer JSON, per‑episode scoring JSON, call cache entry, task manifest, transformation manifest, and analysis output is archived with SHA‑256. Representative artifact SHAs: raw results execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 176776d1...), task manifest execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 91564bb6...), per‑episode example execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256 = 8f38c8be...), analysis paired table analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (SHA‑256 = 3421adb5...), analysis log analysis/analysis_log.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 7db06f53...). The registered analysis executor produced the reported McNemar p and bootstrap CI; its run parameters and seeds are logged (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl).
Autonomy boundary and human roles. The Research Director selected the topic family and approved the master prompt before the autonomy lock. After the autonomy lock the AI autonomously performed literature review, gap selection, preregistration, code generation, experiment execution, artifact archiving, statistical analysis, manuscript drafting, AI‑based peer review, and revision. No manual technical edits of the manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock infrastructure development and rehearsals existed but were not used as empirical evidence; all reported empirical results derive from the archived autonomous run only.
Limitations (short): ceiling baseline (299/300), single‑model scope (gpt‑5‑mini), closed‑world emulator validator proxy, single‑repair budget. Full limitations and per‑artifact references appear in the manuscript body.
limitations: Ceiling baseline: baseline success = 299/300 reduces power to detect large preregistered improvements.
Task scope and external validity: deterministic emulator‑backed intent corpus; results do not directly generalise to noisy, adversarial, or human‑authored intent distributions in production.
Model scope: single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini); no cross‑model generality claimed.
Validator construct validity: safety operationalised as absence of emulator‑observed unintended reachability changes in a closed‑world snapshot; production safety surfaces may be broader.
Repair budget: only a single automated repair attempt was permitted; iterative multi‑call repair strategies were not evaluated in this confirmatory run.
